content: Studies have demonstrated that initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) as soon as an HIV diagnosis is made, ideally within the first weeks of life for infants, can significantly reduce the size of viral reservoirs and limit their formation. However, treating full-term infants younger than two weeks and preterm infants is challenging due to limited data on the pharmacokinetics and appropriate dosing of antiretroviral (ARV) drugs in this age group. This area is currently under active investigation. Adolescents and young women living with HIV face unique challenges in preventing HIV transmission to their children and addressing their own health needs. These challenges include poor access to reproductive health services, low uptake of HIV testing, and poor retention in care. Operational research is urgently needed to identify the factors contributing to poor outcomes in adolescents, develop adolescent-friendly maternal and newborn health services, and create strategies to improve retention in care. While ART during pregnancy and breastfeeding provides clear public health benefits by improving maternal health and preventing transmission to the child, further research is needed to understand the potential adverse effects of ART, particularly during the preconception period, and whether these effects vary between different ART regimens. Current evidence suggests that the risk of congenital birth defects with recommended first-line ARV drugs is similar to that of the general population, but this remains an important area for investigation, especially for newer drugs. Strategies to provide an integrated package of care to reduce overall child mortality are also required. For example, integrating ARV drug delivery into antenatal care and maternal, neonatal, and childcare services, rather than referring patients to separate ART clinics, requires further implementation and assessment. Significant knowledge gaps remain regarding the timing of ART initiation and the optimal ART regimen for newborns, as well as how to safely operationalize ART initiation during the neonatal period amidst competing priorities and limited pharmacokinetic data for optimal drug regimens. Additionally, frontline care providers require appropriate training to address these challenges. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines recommend offering rapid ART initiation to all individuals living with HIV following a confirmed diagnosis and clinical assessment. ART initiation should ideally occur on the same day for those ready to start. Rapid initiation is defined as starting ART within seven days of diagnosis, with priority given to individuals with advanced HIV disease. However, immediate ART initiation is contraindicated in individuals with cryptococcal meningitis due to the increased risk of mortality associated with immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) in the central nervous system. For individuals with suspected tuberculosis (TB), ART should be initiated while rapidly investigating for TB, with close follow-up within seven days to start TB treatment if confirmed. For those with cryptococcal meningitis, ART initiation should be deferred until there is evidence of a sustained clinical response to antifungal therapy, typically after four to six weeks of treatment. Rapid ART initiation has been shown to increase the number of people starting ART, reduce mortality, and decrease mother-to-child transmission and transmission to HIV-negative partners. However, potential harms include missing clinical conditions requiring management before ART, the risk of IRIS in severely immunosuppressed individuals, and the possibility of individuals feeling coerced into starting therapy before they are mentally prepared. Special consideration should be given to women in settings where they may not be able to make independent decisions about starting lifelong therapy. Cost-effectiveness studies from South Africa and China indicate that rapid ART initiation is both cost-effective and sustainable. While additional support may be required to prepare children and their caregivers for ART initiation, particularly when syrups are prescribed, rapid ART initiation is broadly acceptable across most populations. Healthcare workers and program managers report that rapid or same-day initiation is feasible, despite specific challenges in key populations. The availability of rapid diagnostic tests for TB and systems for timely return of results, ideally on the same day, is also critical. Patient education and support for early recognition of IRIS, adverse events, and adherence counseling are necessary. For children living with HIV who are hospitalized or severely ill, studies have assessed the timing of ART initiation. In one South African study, children with severe acute malnutrition were randomized to receive ART within 14 days of admission or after nutritional recovery. In a Kenyan trial, hospitalized children were randomized to start ART within 48 hours versus 7–14 days. Early mortality was extremely high, and urgent ART (within 48 hours) did not improve survival. However, the authors concluded that rapid treatment (whether immediate or within 14 days) is safe, and prompt ART initiation after medical stabilization of coexisting illnesses is essential to reduce the high overall mortality observed. Further research is needed to assess how healthcare systems can adapt to provide rapid or same-day ART initiation in programmatic settings. This includes analyzing clinical readiness assessments, diagnostic and prophylactic interventions for advanced HIV disease, and approaches to support treatment adherence. Research is also needed to evaluate the impact of rapid ART initiation among individuals with TB symptoms, excluding those with meningitis, on mortality, TB and HIV outcomes, adverse events, IRIS, retention in care, and ART adherence. Finally, the role of prophylactic corticosteroids in reducing IRIS incidence among people with TB and HIV in public health settings warrants further investigation.
